hops.afterHeading: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope
hops.title: Why coal in sunshine still looks black
hops.text: It is natural to assume a white object always sends your eye more light than a black one. It does not. White chalk under moonlight sends less light than black coal in direct sunshine, yet chalk still looks white and coal black. Ewald Hering made this point in 1872: without constancy, chalk on a cloudy day would look like coal on a sunny day. Photoreceptors help from the start. Over a range of bright backgrounds, sensitivity falls roughly as one over the background, so they keep signaling changes relative to prevailing light. Later in the pathway, scene comparisons and cues such as surface orientation help judge surface lightness.

sources.citation: Pizlo & de Barros, Front. Comput. Neurosci. 15:681162 (2021)
McCann, Parraman & Rizzi, Front. Psychol. 5:5 (2014), quoting Hering (1872/1905)
Allred & Brainard, J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 26:949-961 (2009)

hops.afterHeading: A second question: when photoreceptors die
hops.title: Too much oxygen after the rods die?
hops.text: When photoreceptors are dying in retinitis pigmentosa, it is tempting to think the retina must be short of oxygen, and hyperbaric oxygen has in fact been used in patients. In two rat models, oxygen microelectrodes pointed the other way. As the dying photoreceptors used less oxygen, oxygen levels rose in what was left of the outer retina, while oxygen tension in the choroid, the blood supply behind the retina, stayed about the same. In transgenic pigs with retinitis pigmentosa, surviving cones show mounting oxidative damage to lipids, proteins and DNA. The authors propose that extra oxygen is what hurts them.

sources.citation: Shen et al., J. Cell. Physiol. 203:457-464 (2005)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A fine glass microelectrode in a positioning stand lowered toward a small sample chamber on a lab bench beside a microscope.
image.caption: In rat models, losing rods leaves more oxygen in the outer retina; extra oxygen may harm surviving cones.

hops.afterHeading: Rescuing vision: what two gene-therapy trials can claim
hops.title: Lancelot the dog and the obstacle course
hops.text: Before any child received RPE65 gene therapy, a shaggy Briard-mix dog named Lancelot helped show it could work. RPE65 mutations in Briards cause an inherited blindness similar to one form of Leber congenital amaurosis. Lancelot was treated with an AAV vector carrying a working RPE65 gene, and the result was reported in 2001. No dog reads an eye chart, so treated dogs were tested on an obstacle course. The results were presented to the U.S. Congress. Early human trials also used a dimly lit obstacle course, and its standardized successor, a mobility test spanning 1 to 400 lux, became the main measure for FDA approval sixteen years later.

sources.citation: Acland et al., Nat. Genet. 28:92-95 (2001); Cheng & Punzo, Hum. Gene Ther. 33:865-878 (2022)
Chung et al., Clin. Exp. Ophthalmol. 46:247-259 (2018)
Cornell Chronicle, 'Gene therapy restores vision in dogs blinded by inherited disease' (April 27, 2001)

image.caption: Treated Briards were tested on an obstacle course; a dim-light mobility test later measured RPE65 gene therapy in people.

audio.title: A Misnamed Protein, a Pacific Atoll and a Briard Named Lancelot
audio.transcript:
Three true stories this time: a protein named for the wrong job, an atoll where an inherited cone disorder became unusually common, and a sheepdog who ran an obstacle course in dim light.

First, the protein. In nineteen ninety-one, a team of biochemists from the Soviet Union and the United States isolated a small, twenty-three-kilodalton calcium-binding protein from photoreceptors. In their assays, lowering calcium seemed to make the preparation speed up c G M P synthesis, which reopens channels and restores the dark state. They published it in Science and named it recoverin. For two years that was the accepted story. Then came an awkward result: the purer the recoverin, the less it stimulated guanylyl cyclase. In nineteen ninety-three the authors published a short note withdrawing the claim. The real cyclase activators soon turned out to be the G caps. Recoverin does sit in the calcium feedback loop, but at the other arrow, holding back G R K one until calcium falls. Nobody changed the name.

Second, the atoll. In the seventeen seventies, a typhoon named Lengkieki struck Pingelap Atoll in Micronesia. The storm and the food shortage that followed left only a few dozen survivors. Family histories trace the condition to one of them, believed to have carried a rare recessive variant in C N G B three, a gene for part of the cone cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel. Over generations on that small, isolated island, the variant became more common. One estimate puts complete achromatopsia at nearly ten percent among Pingelapese people, compared with roughly one in thirty thousand in the general population. With normal cone signaling disrupted, affected people see no color, find bright tropical daylight glaring and hard to see in, and rely on their rods. Nature ran a parallel experiment in Alaskan malamutes. Dogs with a C N G B three deletion become day-blind in bright light, yet see normally in the dim light where rods do the work.

Finally, the sheepdog. Before any child received R P E sixty-five gene therapy, a shaggy Briard-mix dog named Lancelot helped show what it could do. Briards with mutations in R P E sixty-five can inherit a blindness similar to one form of Leber congenital amaurosis in people. Researchers used an A A V vector to deliver a working R P E sixty-five gene beneath Lancelot's retina, and reported the result in two thousand one. You cannot hand a sheepdog an eye chart, so they asked a simpler question: could treated dogs find their way through an obstacle course. The results for these dogs, Lancelot included, were dramatic enough to be presented to the U S Congress. Early human trials also had patients walk a dimly lit obstacle course. A standardized version, the multi-luminance mobility test, repeats the walk at light levels from one lux up to four hundred lux. Sixteen years after Lancelot's result, that test was the main measure behind F D A approval of the treatment.
